resources.string: Visualise the hidden order inside chaos.\nMillions of iterations. Seventeen attractors.\nInfinite shapes waiting to be discovered.
✦ A tribute to the original Chaoscope\nby Nicolas Desprez (2000s) — which first\nmade strange attractors beautiful.
✦ A tribute to the original Chaoscope by Nicolas Desprez
Created by Lucas Balancin and Thiago Sturiale · 2026
Your exported renders will appear here.
A strange attractor slowly rotating on your home screen.
Rotates only while the home screen is visible; pauses in battery saver.
Paste a Chaoscope preset code (CHS1:…) — for example from a shared image caption.
Stretch density so all palette colours show.
Export PNG with transparent BG — great for stickers.
Camera controls are only available for 3D attractors.\n\nSwitch to a 3D attractor on the Shape tab to use yaw, pitch, roll, and depth controls.
Save the current attractor, parameters, camera and look as a reusable preset.
Gamma flattens (lower) or boosts (higher) the brightest regions.
Dims points farther from the camera to bring out 3-D form. 0% is flat.
Plays A→B→A for a seamless looping video.
Trace the orbit up, then erase back to the start.
Morph to the random target and back — seamless loop.
Set Frame A and Frame B to enable export.
Renders the attractor as growing coloured dots — each frame reveals more of the orbit path. No keyframes needed.
Auto-varies all parameters from the current state to a random target — a fresh result every export. No keyframes needed.

Rendering the video can take a while. It keeps running in the background, and we\'ll post a progress notification so you can track it and cancel if needed. Allow notifications on the next screen to see it.
Save the current attractor, parameters, camera and look as a reusable preset.
Shows progress while exporting an animation to MP4.
Drag anywhere on the canvas to rotate the attractor in 3D. Pinch to zoom.
Scroll the thumbnail gallery to pick an attractor — or tap Surprise Me for a random one.
Drag any slider to reshape the orbit in real time. Small changes can completely transform the picture.
The ▶ button in the centre renders your attractor. For a full-resolution image, use HD or 4K in the Export tab.
Switch palette chips to recolour instantly — the live preview updates right away. Tap Edit to build your own gradient.
A classic 2-D iterative map lifted into 3-D. Six knobs warp how each step folds and stretches the orbit — small changes produce wildly different shapes.
Horizontal sine drive — controls the main wave that bends the orbit left and right.
Vertical sine drive — controls how the orbit folds up and down.
Horizontal cosine drive — adds a perpendicular twist to the X axis.
Vertical cosine drive — adds a perpendicular twist to the Y axis.
Coupling between axes — higher values create tighter, more knotted patterns.
Secondary coupling — fine-tunes the overall texture density.
Cousin of Clifford with stronger nonlinearity — produces dense filigree and shell-like layered patterns.
Primary X stretch — wider values pull the orbit horizontally.
Primary Y stretch — wider values pull the orbit vertically.
Secondary X stretch — adds finer-grained horizontal detail.
Secondary Y stretch — adds finer-grained vertical detail.
Final twist — controls how tightly the shape spirals.
A 2-D map from plasma physics. Tends toward delicate, organic curves that look like seashells or jellyfish.
Damping — close to 0 keeps orbits open; further from 0 tightens loops.
Nonlinearity — drives the curl. Negative values flip the spiral direction.
The famous butterfly. Edward Lorenz\'s 1963 weather model — the system that made \"chaos\" a household word.
σ (Prandtl number) — fluid viscosity. Standard value is 10.
ρ (Rayleigh number) — drives the convection. Above ~24.74 the chaos kicks in.
β (aspect ratio) — controls the wing geometry. Standard is 8/3 ≈ 2.667.
dt — simulation step. Smaller = smoother trajectory but slower convergence.
A simpler cousin of Lorenz. Spirals slowly outward then snaps back — like a cosmic pinball.
Inner spiral rate — how fast orbits expand on the flat plane.
Lift offset — small constant that nudges the orbit into 3-D.
Snap threshold — when the orbit reaches this, it folds violently. Higher = wider funnel.
A twisted torus. Loops wrap a central axis while drifting along it — produces shell or Möbius-like shapes.
Twist rate around the axis — higher = tighter coil.
Asymmetry — breaks the perfect torus into more organic curls.
Vertical asymmetry — same idea on the up/down axis.
Cyclically symmetric — the same equation in x, y, and z. Looks like a tangled ball of yarn.
Damping — lower values make the orbit more chaotic. Below ~0.21 it becomes hyperchaotic.
A generic chaotic flow with many control knobs — wide range of forms, from elegant ribbons to dense storms.
Primary drive on the X axis.
Primary drive on the Y axis.
Forcing strength — higher creates more violent dynamics.
Symmetric icons (Field & Golubitsky). Complex polynomials produce mandala-like patterns with rotational symmetry, lifted into a 3-D relief you can tilt and rotate.
λ — overall contraction. More negative pulls orbits inward.
α — radial drive. Higher gives sharper rays.
β — angular distortion. Bends the symmetry axes and the depth relief.
ω — rotation rate. Sets the n-fold symmetry of the final pattern.
Iterated function system. Four affine maps applied at random produce a fractal fern; the twist knob spirals the fronds out of the plane into 3-D.
Width — fattens or thins each leaflet.
Lean — biases the fern left or right of vertical.
Twist — rotates each frond out of plane. 0 is the flat 2-D fern; higher coils it into 3-D.
Quaternion Julia set for q² + c, rendered as a 3-D surface. The j-term (c_j) drives the depth — set it to 0 for the classic flat 2-D Julia.
Imaginary (i) part of c. Values near the Mandelbrot edge give the richest detail.
j part of c — the third dimension. 0 collapses to a flat 2-D Julia; larger values open it into a 3-D body.
Clifford Pickover\'s iconic strange attractor — produces wing- and shell-like 3-D forms with subtle layering.
X stretch — how far the orbit reaches sideways.
Y stretch — vertical span of the shape.
Final twist — sets the overall handedness.
Cyclically symmetric — the same equation cycled through x, y and z. Folds into interlocking torus-knot loops, like a 3-D pretzel.
Damping — lower values loosen the loops; near 1.4 the orbit barely stays bound.
dt — simulation step. Smaller = smoother, slower convergence.
A fast double-spiral that winds into a tight tornado of nested shells — dense, galaxy-like swirls.
Coupling strength — drives the swirl rate. Higher winds the spiral tighter.
Vertical forcing — lifts and stretches the funnel along its axis.
One of Sprott\'s minimal chaotic systems — just two terms, yet it traces a broad swirling disc. Elegant and beginner-friendly.
Coupling — scales the y·z drive that feeds the swirl.
Feedback — scales the x·y term that closes the loop. Reshapes the disc.
Deep blues and purples — cosmic and quiet.
Warm reds, oranges and yellow — molten.
Cool cyan and bright blue — high-voltage.
Greens, teals and violets — northern lights.
Pure luminance — focus on form, not colour.
Full hue wheel — violet through cyan, green, yellow to orange, dark-to-bright.
Deep purple to magenta, orange and golden cream — warm and dramatic.
Navy to steel blue, ice blue and white — cold and crystalline.
Hot pink to electric green — high-contrast, vibrant.
Your own colour stops — tap Edit to customise.
Log-histogram accumulation — the classic Chaoscope mode.
4th-root sparse points — diffuse starfield or dust-cloud look.
Gas with z-buffer depth — near points bright, far points dim.
Cyclic colour bands — high-frequency striped patterns.
Hard threshold silhouette — bold, poster-like fills.
Per-point orbit speed × curvature — warm core, cool periphery, bright at bends.
Maximum detail — an HD render can take a while.
Lightest — smoothest rotation on slower phones.
Most detail while rotating — best on fast phones.
A low-order model of atmospheric circulation — Edward Lorenz\'s 1984 \"weather in a box.\" Traces looping, ribbon-like flows that wander between calm and stormy regimes.
Damping of the westerly wind — how quickly the main flow decays.
Strength of the wave coupling — links the temperature waves to the jet.
Thermal forcing — the equator-to-pole heating that drives the whole system.
Asymmetry forcing — tilts the wave pattern, breaking the symmetry.
The canonical strange attractor — Michel Hénon\'s 1976 map. Its orbit settles onto a delicate banana-shaped curve that, zoomed in, reveals endless self-similar fractal bands.
Nonlinear fold — the squared term that bends the curve. Near 1.4 gives the classic shape; above ~1.42 the orbit escapes.
Contraction — how strongly each step shrinks toward the line. Sets the thickness of the fractal bands.
